title: Café Achteck in Berlin - FAQ
subtitle: What they are, where the 13 survivors stand, and which ones are still open.

items.q: Why are Berlin's green iron urinals called Café Achteck?
items.a: Achteck means **octagon**, after the eight-sided ground plan with seven cast-iron walls and a screened eighth-side entrance. **Café** is classic Berlin humour about popping in to get rid of your coffee, while the city's official type name was **Waidmannslust** for its hunting-green paint.

items.q: How many Café Achteck pavilions are still standing in Berlin?
items.a: Berlin's open-data toilet register and Senate records confirm **11 Café Achtecks still operating as public toilets** in 2026. Including the locked 1914 pavilion on **Huttenstraße** in Moabit and the restored **Museum Reinickendorf** pavilion in Hermsdorf, **13 green octagons** stand outdoors today.

items.q: Do the working Café Achtecks cost money or have opening hours?
items.a: All 11 operating pavilions are listed as **free (0 euros)** and **open 24 hours a day** under Wall GmbH's Berlin toilet contract. Standard modular Berliner Toiletten without outdoor urinals cost **50 cents** cashless, while Café Achtecks and urinals on 107 modern units stay free.

items.q: Can women use a Café Achteck?
items.a: Nine of the eleven operating units remain **men-only standing urinals** with no seated cabin. Two historic frames, at **Rüdesheimer Platz** in Wilmersdorf and **Fellbacher Platz** in Hermsdorf, were rebuilt inside with **two separate seated cabins** for women and men.

items.q: What happened to the Café Achteck on Gendarmenmarkt?
items.a: The green pavilion that used to stand on Gendarmenmarkt was a **2003 replica**, not a 19th-century original. The city removed it in **2019** because of its poor condition and put the shell in storage; a modern **Berliner Toilette** stands nearby instead.

items.q: Is Burgermeister at Schlesisches Tor an old Café Achteck?
items.a: No, although even some city summaries lump them together. The kiosk under the U1 tracks at Schlesisches Tor is a former **rectangular toilet house** built for both sexes, whereas a true **Café Achteck** is an octagonal seven-stall cast-iron urinal designed by Carl Theodor Rospatt.

items.q: Why did Berlin build 142 of them by 1920 and lose most of them?
items.a: They arrived from **1879** right after Berlin opened James Hobrecht's first sewer system, when rapid growth left streets foul. Bombing, post-war division, scrap demolition and the rise of indoor toilets inside cafés and department stores removed nearly all of them after 1945.
